lines.text: Every topic in this chapter so far has quietly assumed something: that you already know which page holds the row you want.
Real tables hold far more rows than fit comfortably in memory, spread across many, many pages.
Checking every one of them in order would work, eventually. What's the structure that makes it unnecessary?
I built a real index on a real, sizeable table and asked Postgres's own page-inspection tools how deep the tree actually is.
Just two levels. Not a comparison for every single row — two.
That's fanout: each page near the top points to many children below it, so the tree's own height grows far slower than the row count does.

lines.text: When a leaf page can't fit a new entry, Postgres splits it: moves part of its contents to a brand new page, and inserts a pointer to that new page in the parent.
If the parent itself is now full, it splits too — the split cascades upward.
Only when even the very top page can't fit a new pointer does the whole tree grow by one more level. That's the one moment fanout actually changes.

lines.text: Worth reasoning through before the measurement settles it.
About to insert a large batch of rows into a brand-new index — should it pack every page as full as it'll go, or leave real room on each page on purpose?
It's not about saving space at any cost — that's the trap.
Packing every page to its limit leaves nothing for a future insert that lands inside an existing page's own range, which forces an immediate split on the very next one.
Leaving real room trades some space up front for genuine room to absorb future writes without splitting.

lines.text: Here's that trade-off shown directly, not just argued for.
The identical batch of inserts, landing inside the existing key range rather than at the end, run against two otherwise identical indexes — one packed tight, one left loose.
Measured directly, the tight index grows by real pages. The loose one, on the exact same data, doesn't grow by a single page.
Duplicates in an indexed column are common — a status flag, a category, a yes-or-no flag.
I built the identical index twice on a column with only a handful of distinct values across many rows: once with a space-saving duplicate representation turned on, once off.
Measured directly, the space-saving version comes out to roughly a third the size of the other.
Here's the part that makes a real index usable under genuinely concurrent writes.
A nineteen-eighty-one algorithm adds just one pointer to every page — to its right-hand sibling — and one more value, an upper bound on what belongs on that page.

If a search's target is bigger than that upper bound, the page must have just split underneath it. The fix isn't a lock on the whole tree — just follow that one pointer to the new page. Postgres's own source implements exactly this.

lines.text: Two more things worth naming precisely, even without a live measurement here.
A newer Postgres release lets a multicolumn index still be used even when a query's own condition skips the very first column, something earlier versions couldn't do.

And a genuinely different design choice in a different engine: clustering a table's actual row data under its primary key means a secondary lookup there costs an extra full tree traversal that a table storing rows separately from its indexes doesn't pay.

lines.text: Pulling the whole topic back together.
Fanout keeps a real index's own depth small no matter how many rows get added, measured directly.

Packing pages tight or loose is a real, measured trade-off, not a guess. A space-saving duplicate representation shrinks a duplicate-heavy index to a fraction its size. And none of it needs to lock the whole tree to stay safe while writes are happening concurrently.

lines.text: One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.

A team sees this topic's own measurement — a space-saving duplicate representation shrank a duplicate-heavy index dramatically — and then redesigns their schema so that same column's values become almost entirely unique.
What happens to that space-saving benefit on the exact same index now?
It shrinks or disappears entirely, and the reason is the same mechanism in reverse.
The entire benefit came from packing tuples that shared identical values into one compact representation.
Once those values stop being duplicates, there's nothing left to pack together — the feature quietly becomes a no-op rather than a space saver.
